Divergent Spirals

GeometryCirclesCurves
Game: Watch a ring of curved lines turn, and see spirals appear that were never drawn.
How to play: Press Start to turn the picture; try Fast or Slow, switch direction, and move the two sliders. You can also drag the outside dot, or focus it and use the arrow keys, to turn it by hand.
Look for the math

This is an optical illusion: a picture made only of arcs convinces your eyes that two spirals are moving. The picture itself never changes shape — only the direction and speed of its turning.

Only circles are drawn

The applet starts with N = 4 and makes its largest radius from the smaller side of the canvas: R = round(min(width, height)/2 − 20), snapped down to a multiple of 4 × (N+1) = 20. On the 640×400 canvas here that gives R = 180. It then draws one arc per ring, using inc = floor(floor(R / floor(360/Opening)) / (N+1)). With the starting Opening = 45° that is inc = 4, so 44 rings are drawn, with radii 4, 8, 12, …, 176.

radius = k,   start = k × Opening,   sweep = Overlap × Opening

Each ring's start is the previous ring's start plus Opening degrees, and each circle is covered for Overlap × Opening degrees — 180° at the defaults. The overlap is what links one ring to the next. The logic test transcribes both nested loops, including all six integer arguments of Java's drawArc, and checks all 17 arc angles × 11 overlaps × 12 canvas sizes: 2,244 configurations, thousands of arcs, no disagreement.

The turn is the trick

After each tick the original adds π/9 radians to the angle in fast mode, or π/17 in slow mode, and waits 10 ms or 20 ms. Counterclockwise subtracts instead of adding. Fast therefore turns (π/9)/10 ÷ (π/17)/20 = 34/9 times as quickly as slow, and the two directions have opposite signs; the test checks this tick by tick up to 64 ticks.

The page asks you to watch a fast clockwise turn and says you will see a dark spiral wind inward and a light one flow outward, while a counterclockwise turn makes both seem to converge. Those are claims about perception, which arithmetic cannot prove: your eyes supply the spirals. What can be checked is the drawing that causes them, and the test verifies it: successive rings are turned by exactly Opening, they span exactly Overlap × Opening, and not one spiral curve is ever drawn.

Little leftovers from the old applet

Two oddities are worth knowing. The applet's own "info" string still calls it Pythagorean Theorem, Proof #36, copied from another applet; it has nothing to do with this picture. It also contains handlers for a third control (the number of concentric arcs, W) that its panel never creates, so W stays at 1 — this page keeps just the two sliders the applet really showed.

Finally, if a canvas is tiny enough that inc = 0, the original loop would never end. This page shows no arcs in that case instead of hanging. At 90° and overlap 11 the requested sweep is 990°, more than a full turn, so both the applet and this page draw a complete circle.

Set the arc angle to 10° and the overlap to 11, then start the rotation: many more, much longer arcs make the effect much stronger.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
